knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Least-Squares Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real ordinary least squares with the half-squared-norm convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For data matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), response \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), and decision vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), the ordinary least-squares loss is
\[L_{\mathrm{OLS}}(x)=\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i)^2.\]
It is a finite-valued convex quadratic function of \(x\), with gradient \(\nabla L_{\mathrm{OLS}}(x)=A^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)\) and Hessian \(\nabla^2L_{\mathrm{OLS}}(x)=A^{\mathsf T}A\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary least squares is half the sum of squared linear residuals. It is a convex quadratic whose Hessian is the positive-semidefinite Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{\mathrm{OLS}}(x)=\tfrac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, derivatives, and convexity claim are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no source citation or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Vector Least-Squares Losses
children.top_down_role: Least-squares templates for vector-valued residual collections.

knowledge_statements.title: Vector Least-Squares Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-squares loss for an affine vector-valued residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\) be affine, with \(F(x)=Ax-b\). The associated vector least-squares loss is
\[L_v(x)=\frac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2=\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2.\]
More generally, for residual vectors \(r_j(x)=A_jx-b_j\), the separable loss \(\frac12\sum_j\lVert r_j(x)\rVert_2^2\) is again a convex quadratic and equals the squared norm of the vertically stacked residual vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector least-squares loss is half the squared Euclidean norm of an affine residual vector; stacked vector residuals give the same template.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=Ax-b\) is affine between finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_v(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\) is a convex quadratic function.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vector-residual definition and stacking statement are precise and appropriate, but they have no supporting citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Least Squares and Linear-Equation Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector least-squares formulation and its exact-versus-approximate interpretation for a linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), the linear least-squares problem is \[p^*=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sum_{j=1}^nA_{ij}x_j-b_i\right)^2=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\|Ax-b\|_2^2.\] The system \(Ax=b\) has a solution if and only if \(p^*=0\). Otherwise, a least-squares minimizer provides an approximate solution minimizing the squared residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear least squares minimizes the squared residual of a linear system. The system is exactly solvable precisely when the minimum residual is zero; otherwise a minimizer gives a minimum-residual approximation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\|Ax-b\|_2^2;\qquad (\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b)\iff p^*=0
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Least Squares and Linear-Equation Residuals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the vector-residual least-squares model with at least as many residuals as variables. No full-rank assumption on the coefficient matrix is stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^k\), and \(k\ge n\), an unconstrained linear least-squares problem with variable \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\;\|Ax-b\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^k(a_i^Tx-b_i)^2,\] where \(a_i^T\) is the \(i\)-th row of \(A\); the problem has no constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a real k-by-n matrix A with k at least n and a vector b, an unconstrained linear least-squares problem minimizes the squared Euclidean norm of Ax minus b, equivalently the sum of the squared affine residuals, over x in R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \|Ax-b\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^k(a_i^Tx-b_i)^2\quad\text{with no constraints}

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Least-Squares Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frobenius least squares for an affine matrix-valued residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A:\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\to\mathbb{R}^{r\times s}\) be linear and let \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times s}\). The matrix least-squares loss is
\[L_M(X)=\frac12\lVert\mathcal A(X)-C\rVert_F^2=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{s}\bigl(\mathcal A(X)_{ij}-C_{ij}\bigr)^2.\]
Because the squared Frobenius norm is convex and \(\mathcal A(X)-C\) is affine, \(L_M\) is a convex quadratic function of the entries of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix least squares squares and sums every entry of an affine matrix residual, equivalently taking half its squared Frobenius norm.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a linear map between finite-dimensional real matrix spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_M(X)=\tfrac12\lVert\mathcal A(X)-C\rVert_F^2\) is convex in \(X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Frobenius least-squares definition is mathematically sound and fits the matrix-loss leaf, but no source or specific locator is provided.

children.title: Vectorization Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between matrix residual organization and vectorized least-squares loss organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Vectorization Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of Frobenius least squares to vector least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every matrix \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times s}\), column-wise vectorization preserves the Frobenius norm:
\[\lVert R\rVert_F=\lVert\operatorname{vec}(R)\rVert_2.\]
Consequently, if \(R(X)=AXB-C\) with compatible real matrices, then
\[\frac12\lVert AXB-C\rVert_F^2=\frac12\left\lVert(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)-\operatorname{vec}(C)\right\rVert_2^2,\]
where the identity \(\operatorname{vec}(AXB)=(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)\) is used. Thus the matrix and vector formulations have identical objective values under vectorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vectorizing a matrix residual converts its Frobenius norm exactly into a Euclidean norm; two-sided matrix multiplication becomes a Kronecker-product linear map.
assumptions_latex: \(A,X,B,C\) are real matrices of compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tfrac12\lVert AXB-C\rVert_F^2=\tfrac12\lVert(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)-\operatorname{vec}(C)\rVert_2^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vectorization and Kronecker-product identities are correctly stated, but the representation has no authoritative citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Least-Squares Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite weighting of a real affine residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For residual \(r(x)=Ax-b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\) and symmetric weight matrix \(W\in\mathbb{S}_+^{m}\), the weighted least-squares loss is
\[L_W(x)=\frac12r(x)^{\mathsf T}Wr(x)=\frac12\lVert W^{1/2}(Ax-b)\rVert_2^2.\]
It is convex in \(x\), with Hessian \(A^{\mathsf T}WA\succeq0\). If \(W\succ0\), every residual direction is penalized; if \(W\) is singular, residual components in \(\ker W\) incur zero loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted least squares measures an affine residual in a positive-semidefinite quadratic metric. Singular weights leave residual directions in the weight’s nullspace unpenalized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_W(x)=\tfrac12(Ax-b)^{\mathsf T}W(Ax-b)\) is convex in \(x\).

notation.meaning: symmetric positive-semidefinite square root of W

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-semidefinite weighted loss, square-root representation, Hessian, and nullspace observation are coherent, but no source evidence is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Least-Squares Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least squares weighted by the inverse error covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the linear model \(b=Ax+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\) has zero mean and covariance \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{m}\). The generalized least-squares loss is
\[L_{\mathrm{GLS}}(x)=\frac12(Ax-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(Ax-b)=\frac12\lVert\Sigma^{-1/2}(Ax-b)\rVert_2^2.\]
Thus GLS is ordinary least squares applied to the whitened system \(\Sigma^{-1/2}Ax\approx\Sigma^{-1/2}b\), and it is a convex quadratic with Hessian \(A^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}A\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized least squares weights correlated residuals by the inverse covariance, equivalently applying ordinary least squares after whitening the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{\mathrm{GLS}}(x)=\tfrac12\lVert\Sigma^{-1/2}(Ax-b)\rVert_2^2\) is convex in \(x\).

notation.meaning: inverse symmetric square root used for whitening

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-covariance GLS definition and whitening representation are standard and locally appropriate, but they lack a cited source and locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Heteroscedastic Quadratic Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal inverse-variance scaling for uncorrelated heteroscedastic errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose residual components are uncorrelated and have positive variances \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma_i^2\). Then \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_m^2)\), and the generalized least-squares loss reduces to
\[L(x)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{(a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i)^2}{\sigma_i^2}=\frac12\lVert D(Ax-b)\rVert_2^2,\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_m^{-1}).\]
Hence each squared residual is scaled by its precision \(\sigma_i^{-2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For uncorrelated errors with unequal positive variances, generalized least squares divides each squared residual by its variance, so higher-variance observations receive less weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(x)=\tfrac12\sum_i\sigma_i^{-2}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i)^2=\tfrac12\lVert D(Ax-b)\rVert_2^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Objective Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expansion of least squares into standard convex quadratic-objective form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), expansion gives
\[\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2=\frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+c,\qquad Q=A^{\mathsf T}A,\quad q=-A^{\mathsf T}b,\quad c=\frac12b^{\mathsf T}b.\]
Because \(Q\succeq0\), minimizing this objective over a convex feasible set is a convex optimization problem with a quadratic objective. When the feasible set is described by affine equalities and inequalities, this is a convex quadratic program. The constant \(c\) may be omitted without changing the minimizers or comparisons between feasible objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding the squared residual produces a convex quadratic objective with Gram Hessian. Over affine constraints it gives a convex quadratic program, and its constant term can be dropped without changing minimizers.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set, if present, is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tfrac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax-(A^{\mathsf T}b)^{\mathsf T}x+\tfrac12b^{\mathsf T}b\).

children.title: Norm-Based Modeling Route
children.top_down_role: Least-squares modeling through a residual-norm interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Based Modeling Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct convex modeling with the Euclidean residual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be nonempty. The norm-based least-squares route solves
\[\underset{x\in C}{\operatorname{minimize}}\;\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2.\]
The objective is convex because it is a norm composed with an affine map. Since the scalar function \(t\mapsto\frac12t^2\) is strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\), this problem has exactly the same minimizers as minimizing \(\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2\) over \(C\), although their optimal objective values use different scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One may minimize the Euclidean residual norm directly. Because squaring is strictly increasing for nonnegative values, this route has the same minimizers as least squares.
assumptions_latex: The same feasible set \(C\) is used in both formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotone-transformation argument correctly establishes equality of argmin sets and fits the modeling-route leaf, but no source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Epigraph Modeling Route
children.top_down_role: Least-squares modeling through an auxiliary epigraph interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Modeling Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone epigraph formulation of residual-norm minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty feasible set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\), the residual-norm problem has the epigraph formulation
\[\underset{x,t}{\operatorname{minimize}}\;t\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\in C,\qquad \lVert Ax-b\rVert_2\le t.\]
The norm inequality is a second-order-cone constraint, equivalently \((t,Ax-b)\in\mathcal Q^{m+1}\), where \(\mathcal Q^{m+1}=\{(t,u):\lVert u\rVert_2\le t\}\). At every optimum, \(t=\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introduce a scalar upper bound on the residual norm and minimize it. The resulting norm inequality is a second-order-cone constraint tight at optimum.
assumptions_latex: The epigraph problem attains an optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2=\min\{t:x\in C,\ (t,Ax-b)\in\mathcal Q^{m+1}\}\).

notation.meaning: epigraph variable bounding the residual norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm epigraph and second-order-cone representation are correct under the stated attainment assumption, but they lack supporting evidence and an inspectable locator.

children.title: Route Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between norm-based and epigraph formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Route Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of squared-loss, norm, and norm-epigraph routes at the optimizer level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be nonempty. Suppose the displayed minima are attained. Then
\[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2=\left\{x\in C:\exists t\in\mathbb{R}\text{ such that }(x,t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{y\in C,\ s\in\mathbb{R}\\ \lVert Ay-b\rVert_2\le s}}s\right\}.\]
If the common minimum residual norm is \(\rho\), the norm and epigraph optimal values equal \(\rho\), while the squared-loss optimal value equals \(\rho^2/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared-loss, residual-norm, and norm-epigraph formulations select exactly the same feasible x-minimizers; only their reported optimal objective values differ by squaring and scaling.
assumptions_latex: All three optimization problems attain their minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three formulations have identical minimizing \(x\), with optimal values \(\rho^2/2\), \(\rho\), and \(\rho\), respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Algebra Solution Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact unconstrained least-squares solution through a compact singular value decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\). Initialize no iterate; compute a compact singular value decomposition \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), where \(r=\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and \(\Sigma_r\) has positive diagonal entries. Set
\[x_{\min}=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{\mathsf T}b=A^{\dagger}b.\]
Stop after this factorization and return \(x_{\min}\), the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution. The complete solution set is
\[\left\{A^{\dagger}b+(I-A^{\dagger}A)z:z\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a compact SVD and apply the pseudoinverse to obtain the minimum-norm least-squares solution; adding any nullspace component gives every solution.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic and the singular value decomposition are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{\min}=A^{\dagger}b\) minimizes \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2\) and has minimum Euclidean norm among all minimizers.

notation.meaning: compact singular value decomposition of A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-SVD pseudoinverse algorithm, minimum-norm conclusion, and complete least-squares solution set are appropriate for this solution-route leaf, but no authoritative source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Residual Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar least-absolute-deviations loss and its empirical aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an observed response \(y\in\mathbb{R}\) and prediction \(\hat y\in\mathbb{R}\), define the residual by \(r=y-\hat y\). The absolute residual loss is \(\ell_{\mathrm{abs}}(y,\hat y)=|y-\hat y|=|r|\). For observations \((x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\) and a predictor \(f\), the empirical least-absolute-deviations objective is \(L(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i-f(x_i)|\), or \(n^{-1}L(f)\) under mean-loss normalization. The function \(r\mapsto |r|\) is convex and finite on \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute loss is the magnitude of a scalar prediction residual; least-absolute-deviations fitting minimizes the sum or mean of these magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{abs}}(y,\hat y)=|y-\hat y|\) and \(L(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n|y_i-f(x_i)|\) are convex in affine predictions.

notation.meaning: response residual, equal to observed minus predicted response

knowledge_statements.title: Median-Regression Target
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population characterization of least-absolute-deviations prediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be an integrable real random variable and define \(R(a)=\mathbb{E}|Y-a|\) for \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(a\) minimizes \(R\) if and only if it is a median of \(Y\), meaning \(\mathbb{P}(Y\le a)\ge \tfrac12\) and \(\mathbb{P}(Y\ge a)\ge \tfrac12\). Conditionally, for a pair \((X,Y)\), any measurable predictor \(f\) satisfying \(f(x)\in\operatorname{Med}(Y\mid X=x)\) almost surely minimizes \(\mathbb{E}|Y-f(X)|\) among measurable predictors for which the expectation is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected absolute loss targets a median; conditional absolute-loss regression targets a conditional median of the response.
assumptions_latex: Conditional medians admit a measurable selection in the regression statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}|Y-a|=\operatorname{Med}(Y)\).

notation.meaning: population absolute-loss risk at prediction a

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Loss Epigraph Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear epigraph formulation of a finite least-absolute-deviations objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let residuals be affine functions \(r_i(z)=a_i^{\mathsf T}z-b_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), and let \(Z\) be any feasible set. Introducing epigraph variables \(t_i\in\mathbb{R}\) gives the equivalent formulation \[\min_{z\in Z}\sum_{i=1}^n |r_i(z)|=\min_{z\in Z,\,t\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n t_i:\ -t_i\le r_i(z)\le t_i,\ i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.\] At every optimum, \(t_i=|r_i(z)|\). If \(Z\) is polyhedral, the right-hand problem is a linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each absolute residual is replaced by an epigraph variable bounded below by both signed residuals, producing an equivalent linear program over polyhedral constraints.
assumptions_latex: The original feasible set \(Z\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed epigraph problem has the same optimal value and optimal \(z\)-solutions as \(\min_{z\in Z}\sum_i|r_i(z)|\).

notation.meaning: epigraph variable for the magnitude of residual i
feasible set for the decision vector

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Quantile Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pinball loss for one prescribed conditional quantile level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\tau\in(0,1)\). For response \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), prediction \(q\in\mathbb{R}\), and residual \(u=y-q\), the single-quantile pinball loss is \[\rho_\tau(u)=u\bigl(\tau-\mathbf{1}_{\{u<0\}}\bigr)=\tau\max\{u,0\}+(1-\tau)\max\{-u,0\}.\] Its population risk is \(R_\tau(q)=\mathbb{E}\rho_\tau(Y-q)\). Whenever this expectation is finite, its minimizers are precisely the \(\tau\)-quantiles in the generalized sense \(\mathbb{P}(Y<q)\le\tau\le\mathbb{P}(Y\le q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pinball loss penalizes underprediction with slope τ and overprediction with slope 1−τ; its population minimizers are generalized τ-quantiles.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is real-valued and the displayed risk is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\mathbb{R}}R_\tau(q)=\{q:\mathbb{P}(Y<q)\le\tau\le\mathbb{P}(Y\le q)\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard pinball-loss definition and generalized quantile characterization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pinball-loss definition, generalized quantile condition, and content kind fit the leaf, but no authoritative source with a specific locator supports the definition and minimizer characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Quantile Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-tail specialization of pinball loss; lower tails follow by reversing the level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an upper-tail level \(\tau\in(\tfrac12,1)\), define the tail-quantile loss for residual \(u=y-q\) by \[\rho_\tau(u)=\tau\max\{u,0\}+(1-\tau)\max\{-u,0\}.\] Thus a positive residual, representing underprediction of \(y\), receives the larger slope \(\tau\). Minimizing \(\mathbb{E}\rho_\tau(Y-q)\) over \(q\in\mathbb{R}\) targets the generalized upper \(\tau\)-quantile set \(\{q:\mathbb{P}(Y<q)\le\tau\le\mathbb{P}(Y\le q)\}\). Lower-tail loss is obtained by taking \(\tau\in(0,\tfrac12)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tail pinball loss uses an extreme quantile level, weighting errors asymmetrically so that its risk targets an upper or lower tail quantile.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer of \(q\mapsto\mathbb{E}\rho_\tau(Y-q)\) is a generalized upper \(\tau\)-quantile, and conversely.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct upper-tail specialization of standard pinball loss
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The upper-tail specialization is internally consistent, but the convention identifying all levels above one half as tail levels and the quantile-targeting claim lack an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Quantile Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint weighted pinball objective for finitely many quantile levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K<1\) and weights \(w_k>0\). For response \(y\in\mathbb{R}\) and predicted quantiles \(q=(q_1,\ldots,q_K)\), define \[L(y,q)=\sum_{k=1}^K w_k\rho_{\tau_k}(y-q_k),\qquad \rho_\tau(u)=\tau\max\{u,0\}+(1-\tau)\max\{-u,0\}.\] The loss is convex and separable in \(q\). Monotone predicted quantiles may be enforced by the convex constraints \(q_1\le\cdots\le q_K\); these constraints prevent crossing but can couple the otherwise separate quantile fits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple-quantile loss sums weighted pinball losses across ordered levels, optionally imposing noncrossing constraints on their predicted quantiles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\mapsto L(y,q)\) is convex, and \(\{q:q_1\le\cdots\le q_K\}\) is a convex noncrossing feasible set.

notation.meaning: positive weight assigned to level k

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Graph Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-of-affine representation of the pinball-loss graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\tau\in(0,1)\), the pinball loss has the piecewise-linear representation \[\rho_\tau(u)=\begin{cases}\tau u,&u\ge0,\\(\tau-1)u,&u<0,\end{cases}\qquad =\max\{\tau u,(\tau-1)u\}.\] Consequently its epigraph is \[\operatorname{epi}\rho_\tau=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:t\ge\tau u,\ t\ge(\tau-1)u\}.\] For an affine residual \(u(z)\), composing these two affine graph pieces with \(u(z)\) yields a convex piecewise-linear loss in \(z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Programming Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-program formulation of finite-sample quantile regression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\), \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\tau\in(0,1)\), write each residual as \(y-X\beta=u^+-u^-\) with \(u^+,u^-\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\). knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Absolute-Residual Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform or minimax loss over a finite residual vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a residual vector \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the maximum absolute-residual loss is \[L_\infty(r)=\max_{1\le i\le n}|r_i|=\|r\|_\infty.\] If \(r_i(z)=a_i^{\mathsf T}z-b_i\) are affine, minimizing this loss is equivalent to \[\min_{z,t}\{t:-t\le r_i(z)\le t\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\] The objective controls the worst residual uniformly; it is convex, positively homogeneous, and a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum absolute-residual loss is the infinity norm of the residual vector and measures the worst fitting error.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Uniform Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted minimax loss for heterogeneous residual scales or priorities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and weights \(w_i>0\). knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Insensitivity Tube
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard epsilon-insensitive scalar residual loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Insensitive-Loss Epigraph Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear epigraph formulation of the scalar epsilon-insensitive residual loss.

(r,t)\in\operatorname{epi}\rho_\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
t\ge 0,\qquad t\ge r-\varepsilon,\qquad t\ge-r-\varepsilon.
\]
Consequently, replacing each objective term \(\rho_\varepsilon(r_i)\) by a variable \(t_i\) and these three inequalities gives an equivalent convex-programming formulation when \(t_i\) is minimized.

knowledge_statements.title: Central Quadratic Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local form of the scalar Huber loss inside its threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a threshold \(\delta>0\), let
\[
h_\delta(r)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12 r^2,& |r|\le\delta,\\
\delta|r|-\tfrac12\delta^2,& |r|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
On the central interval \([-\delta,\delta]\), the loss is exactly quadratic: \(h_\delta(r)=\tfrac12r^2\), with derivative \(h_\delta'(r)=r\) and second derivative \(h_\delta''(r)=1\) for \(|r|<\delta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Tail Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tail form and bounded slope of the scalar Huber loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Huber loss
\[
h_\delta(r)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12r^2,& |r|\le\delta,\\
\delta|r|-\tfrac12\delta^2,& |r|>\delta,
\end{cases}
\qquad \delta>0,
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Scale Huber Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard scalar Huber loss with a prescribed, optimization-independent threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a fixed threshold \(\delta>0\), the fixed-scale Huber loss is the function \(h_\delta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R_+\) defined by
\[
h_\delta(r)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12r^2,& |r|\le\delta,\\
\delta|r|-\tfrac12\delta^2,& |r|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
The two pieces agree in value and first derivative at \(r=\pm\delta\); thus \(h_\delta\) is convex and continuously differentiable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Huber representation of a smoothed location objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a fixed-scale Huber-type smoothing of a population-weighted sum of norms through a regularized dual maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb E_2=(\mathbb E_1^*)^p\),
\[
Q_2=\{u=(u_1,\ldots,u_p):\|u_j\|_{\mathbb E_1}^*\leq1\ \text{for all }j\},
\]
\[
\|u\|_{\mathbb E_2}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^p m_j(\|u_j\|_{\mathbb E_1}^*)^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad d_2(u)=\tfrac12\|u\|_{\mathbb E_2}^2.
\]
For \(\mu>0\), define
\[
f_\mu(x)=\max_{u\in Q_2}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^p m_j\langle u_j,x-c_j\rangle-\mu d_2(u)\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
f_\mu(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p m_j\psi_\mu(\|x-c_j\|_{\mathbb E_1}),
\]
where
\[
\psi_\mu(\tau)=\max_{0\leq\gamma\leq1}\left\{\gamma\tau-\tfrac12\mu\gamma^2\right\}=
\begin{cases}
\tau^2/(2\mu),&0\leq\tau\leq\mu,\\
\tau-\mu/2,&\tau\geq\mu.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic regularization of the dual unit-ball representation of the weighted location objective yields a separable fixed-scale Huber function. Each distance term is quadratic up to mu and linear beyond mu.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_\mu(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p m_j\psi_\mu(\|x-c_j\|_{\mathbb E_1}),\quad \psi_\mu(\tau)=\begin{cases}\tau^2/(2\mu),&0\leq\tau\leq\mu,\\\tau-\mu/2,&\tau\geq\mu.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Normalized Huber Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-equivariant Huber loss obtained by standardizing a residual and restoring squared units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h_\delta\) denote the fixed-scale Huber loss, let \(\sigma>0\) be a residual scale, and let \(\delta>0\) be dimensionless. The scale-normalized loss is
\[
H_{\sigma,\delta}(r)=\sigma^2h_\delta(r/\sigma)
=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12r^2,& |r|\le\sigma\delta,\\
\sigma\delta|r|-\tfrac12\sigma^2\delta^2,& |r|>\sigma\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
It satisfies \(H_{a\sigma,\delta}(ar)=a^2H_{\sigma,\delta}(r)\) for every \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standardize by the residual scale, apply Huber loss, and multiply by squared scale to preserve squared-loss units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_{\sigma,\delta}(r)=\sigma^2h_\delta(r/\sigma)\) and \(H_{a\sigma,\delta}(ar)=a^2H_{\sigma,\delta}(r)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Huber Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Huber loss whose threshold is selected from data or an external iteration state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) denote observed data or an external algorithmic state, and let \(\tau(D)>0\) be chosen without dependence on the residual variable \(r\). The adaptive Huber loss is
\[
h_{\tau(D)}(r)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12r^2,& |r|\le\tau(D),\\
\tau(D)|r|-\tfrac12\tau(D)^2,& |r|>\tau(D).
\end{cases}
\]
Conditional on \(D\), it is convex in \(r\). If \(\tau\) is jointly optimized, this conditional convexity alone does not establish joint convexity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\mapsto h_{\tau(D)}(r)\) is convex for each fixed \(D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Huber Epigraph Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted epigraph formulation derived from the scalar Huber infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta>0\), a pair \((r,t)\in\mathbb R^2\) belongs to the epigraph of \(h_\delta\) if and only if there exist \(z\in\mathbb R\) and \(s,q\ge0\) such that
\[
s\ge z,\qquad s\ge-z,\qquad q\ge\tfrac12(r-z)^2,
\qquad t\ge q+\delta s.
\]
Indeed, minimizing the right-hand bound over \(z,s,q\) yields \(\inf_z\{\tfrac12(r-z)^2+\delta|z|\}=h_\delta(r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Huber epigraph is represented using an absolute-value lift and one convex quadratic epigraph constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((r,t)\in\operatorname{epi}h_\delta\) exactly when the displayed lifted constraints are feasible.

notation.meaning: epigraph variable for the quadratic term

knowledge_statements.title: Huber Conic Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone formulation of the lifted scalar Huber epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the rotated second-order cone by
\[
\mathcal Q_r^3=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:2uv\ge w^2,\ u\ge0,\ v\ge0\}.
\]
For \(\delta>0\), the condition \(t\ge h_\delta(r)\) is equivalent to the existence of \(z\in\mathbb R\) and \(s,q\ge0\) satisfying
\[
s\ge z,\qquad s\ge-z,\qquad (q,1,r-z)\in\mathcal Q_r^3,
\qquad t\ge q+\delta s.
\]
Thus the Huber epigraph is second-order-cone representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated second-order cone represents the quadratic part of the lifted Huber epigraph exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge h_\delta(r)\) is equivalent to feasibility of the displayed conic system.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal-Convolution Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Huber loss as the infimal convolution of a quadratic and a scaled absolute value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta>0\), let \(q(r)=\tfrac12r^2\) and \(g(r)=\delta|r|\) on \(\mathbb R\). Their infimal convolution is
\[
(q\mathbin{\square}g)(r)
=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}\left\{\tfrac12(r-z)^2+\delta|z|\right\}.
\]
For every \(r\in\mathbb R\), this infimum is attained and equals the Huber loss \(h_\delta(r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Huber loss is the infimal convolution of half the squared residual and the delta-scaled absolute value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_\delta=q\mathbin{\square}(\delta|\cdot|)\).

notation.meaning: infimal convolution of f and g

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Huber loss as the unit-parameter Moreau envelope of the scaled absolute value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define its unit-parameter Moreau envelope by
\[
e_1g(r)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}\left\{g(z)+\tfrac12(r-z)^2\right\}.
\]
Taking \(g(z)=\delta|z|\) with \(\delta>0\) gives
\[
e_1(\delta|\cdot|)(r)=h_\delta(r)
\]
for every \(r\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Huber loss is the Moreau envelope, with parameter one, of the delta-scaled absolute-value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_\delta=e_1(\delta|\cdot|)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of the Huber piecewise, infimal-convolution, and Moreau-envelope formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta>0\) and \(r\in\mathbb R\), the minimizer in
\[
\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}\left\{\tfrac12(r-z)^2+\delta|z|\right\}
\]
is \(z^*=\operatorname{sign}(r)(|r|-\delta)_+\). Substitution yields
\[
e_1(\delta|\cdot|)(r)
=(q\mathbin{\square}(\delta|\cdot|))(r)
=h_\delta(r)
=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12r^2,& |r|\le\delta,\\
\delta|r|-\tfrac12\delta^2,& |r|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft thresholding evaluates the infimal convolution, proving that its envelope value is exactly the piecewise Huber loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_1(\delta|\cdot|)=q\mathbin{\square}(\delta|\cdot|)=h_\delta\).

notation.meaning: quadratic function equal to half of r squared

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Huber Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth convex approximation to Huber loss with quadratic center and asymptotically linear tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta>0\), the pseudo-Huber loss is \(p_\delta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R_+\) defined by
\[
p_\delta(r)=\delta^2\left(\sqrt{1+(r/\delta)^2}-1\right).
\]
It is infinitely differentiable and convex, with
\[
p_\delta'(r)=\frac{r}{\sqrt{1+(r/\delta)^2}},
\qquad
p_\delta''(r)=\left(1+(r/\delta)^2\right)^{-3/2}>0.
\]
Moreover, \(p_\delta(r)=\tfrac12r^2+o(r^2)\) as \(r\to0\), while \(p_\delta(r)/|r|\to\delta\) as \(|r|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-Huber is a smooth strictly convex loss that is locally quadratic and asymptotically linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_\delta\) is smooth and strictly convex, with quadratic center and tail slope magnitude approaching \(\delta\).

notation.meaning: term negligible relative to squared r near zero

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula, derivatives, strict convexity, local expansion, and asymptotic tail slope are mathematically consistent, and definition fits the leaf. Pseudo-Huber normalizations vary, so the absent citation and locator must be supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Quantile-Huber Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau smoothing of the quantile check loss, with smoothing parameter \(\kappa>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\tau\in(0,1)\), define the check loss by \(\rho_\tau(u)=\tau u\) when \(u\ge 0\) and \(\rho_\tau(u)=(\tau-1)u\) when \(u<0\). The quantile-Huber loss is
\[Q_{\tau,\kappa}(r)=\inf_{u\in\mathbb R}\left\{\rho_\tau(u)+\frac{(r-u)^2}{2\kappa}\right\}=\begin{cases}(\tau-1)r-\frac{\kappa(1-\tau)^2}{2},&r<-\kappa(1-\tau),\\ \frac{r^2}{2\kappa},&-\kappa(1-\tau)\le r\le\kappa\tau,\\ \tau r-\frac{\kappa\tau^2}{2},&r>\kappa\tau.\end{cases}\]
It is convex and continuously differentiable in \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quantile-Huber loss quadratically smooths the quantile check loss near zero while retaining its asymmetric linear tails.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Huber Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper- and lower-tail Huber penalties obtained from positive and negative residual parts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r_+=\max\{r,0\}\) and let
\[H_\delta(s)=\begin{cases}\frac{s^2}{2},&0\le s\le\delta,\\ \delta s-\frac{\delta^2}{2},&s>\delta.\end{cases}\]
The upper- and lower-sided Huber losses are respectively \(H_\delta^+(r)=H_\delta(r_+)\) and \(H_\delta^-(r)=H_\delta((-r)_+)\). Thus \(H_\delta^+\) penalizes only positive residuals and \(H_\delta^-\) only negative residuals; each is convex and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two losses apply a quadratic-to-linear Huber penalty exclusively to the positive or negative part of a residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_\delta^+\) and \(H_\delta^-\) are nonnegative, convex, and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Margin Logistic Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary logistic loss expressed through a signed classification margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a binary label \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) and a real-valued score \(f\), the signed margin is \(m=yf\). The signed-margin logistic loss is
\[\ell_{\mathrm{log}}(y,f)=\log\!\left(1+e^{-yf}\right)=\log\!\left(1+e^{-m}\right).\]
As a function of \(f\), it is finite, convex, nonnegative, and strictly decreasing in the signed margin \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary logistic loss is the softplus of the negative signed margin: correctly classified examples with larger margins incur smaller loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{log}}(y,f)=\log(1+e^{-yf})\) is convex in \(f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Probability Log Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bernoulli negative log-likelihood for probability-valued predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a label \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and predicted probability \(p\in(0,1)\), the binary probability log loss is
\[\ell_{\mathrm{bin}}(y,p)=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p).\]
Its lower-semicontinuous extension to \(p\in[0,1]\) uses \(-\log 0=+\infty\) and \(0\log 0=0\). For fixed \(y\), the loss is convex in \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary log loss is the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the observed class, with infinite loss for assigning it zero probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{bin}}(y,p)=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p)\) is convex and lower semicontinuous in \(p\).
review_flags: Standard definition, but no supplied locator directly supports binary probability log loss.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bernoulli log-loss formula and its lower-semicontinuous endpoint extension are precise and appropriate, but no cited source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Binary Logistic Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class-weighted binary logistic loss in probability and score parameterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(w_0,w_1\ge0\) be class weights, not both zero. For \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p\in(0,1)\), define
\[\ell_w(y,p)=-w_1y\log p-w_0(1-y)\log(1-p).\]
Under the logit parameterization \(p=(1+e^{-f})^{-1}\), this equals
\[\ell_w(y,f)=w_1y\log(1+e^{-f})+w_0(1-y)\log(1+e^f).\]
For fixed \(y\), both displayed forms are convex in their respective scalar arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted logistic loss multiplies each class-specific log loss by a nonnegative cost, allowing asymmetric treatment of the two classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_w(y,p)\) is convex in \(p\), and \(\ell_w(y,f)\) is convex in \(f\).
review_flags: Standard weighted form, but no supplied locator directly supports its normalization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probability and logit parameterizations agree and are convex in their stated arguments. The definition fits the leaf, but the weighting convention and normalization lack a cited authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Softmax Cross-Entropy Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiclass negative log-likelihood for an unrestricted vector of class scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(K\ge2\), a score vector \(z\in\mathbb R^K\), and observed class \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), define softmax probabilities \(p_k(z)=e^{z_k}/\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}\). The softmax cross-entropy loss is
\[\ell_{\mathrm{sm}}(y,z)=-\log p_y(z)=\log\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}\right)-z_y.\]
It is convex in \(z\) and is unchanged when the same scalar is added to every component of \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Softmax cross-entropy is the negative log probability assigned to the observed class and is convex in the class-score vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{sm}}(y,z)=\log(\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j})-z_y\) is convex in \(z\).
review_flags: Standard definition, but no supplied locator directly supports softmax cross-entropy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The softmax cross-entropy formula, convexity claim, and common-shift invariance are correct and match the leaf. No source reference or specific locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Class Logistic Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiable multiclass logistic loss with the final class fixed as the zero-score reference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\ge2\), choose class \(K\) as reference, and set \(z_K=0\) while \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_{K-1})\in\mathbb R^{K-1}\). For \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), the reference-class logistic loss is
\[\ell_{\mathrm{ref}}(y,z)=\log\!\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}e^{z_j}\right)-\mathbf 1_{\{y<K\}}z_y.\]
This is the softmax cross-entropy under the reference constraint and is convex in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reference-class logistic loss removes softmax score nonidentifiability by fixing one class score to zero and optimizing the remaining scores.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{ref}}(y,z)\) is convex in the \(K-1\) free scores.

knowledge_statements.title: One-versus-Rest Logistic Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sum of independent binary logistic losses for multiclass indicator targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(K\ge2\), class scores \(f\in\mathbb R^K\), and observed class \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), set \(s_k(y)=1\) if \(k=y\) and \(s_k(y)=-1\) otherwise. The one-versus-rest logistic loss is
\[\ell_{\mathrm{OvR}}(y,f)=\sum_{k=1}^K\log\!\left(1+e^{-s_k(y)f_k}\right).\]
Each summand is a binary signed-margin logistic loss, so the aggregate loss is convex in \(f\); its independently fitted probabilities need not sum to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-versus-rest logistic loss sums K binary logistic losses, treating the observed class as positive and every other class as negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{OvR}}(y,f)\) is convex and separable in the coordinates of \(f\).

notation.meaning: score for the kth one-versus-rest classifier

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Sum-Exp Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logistic losses represented as affine terms plus a log-sum-exp atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\operatorname{lse}(a)=\log(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{a_i})\) for \(a\in\mathbb R^m\). Then binary signed-margin logistic loss and multiclass softmax loss admit the canonical representations
\[\log(1+e^{-m})=\operatorname{lse}(0,-m),\qquad \ell_{\mathrm{sm}}(y,z)=\operatorname{lse}(z)-z_y.\]
Because log-sum-exp is convex and composition with an affine map preserves convexity, these formulas provide convex-programming representations of both losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary and multiclass logistic losses are affine transformations of the convex log-sum-exp atom.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in\mathbb R^K\) and \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\) in the multiclass identity
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log(1+e^{-m})=\operatorname{lse}(0,-m)\) and \(\ell_{\mathrm{sm}}(y,z)=\operatorname{lse}(z)-z_y\).
review_flags: Standard identities, but no supplied locator directly supports the canonical representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The log-sum-exp identities are correct, and representation is the appropriate content kind for this canonical-route leaf. No supporting source or specific locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Cone Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic epigraph representation of log-sum-exp and hence logistic losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the closed exponential cone be \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ y e^{x/y}\le z\}\). For \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), the log-sum-exp epigraph has the exact representation
\[t\ge\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{a_i}\right)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists u\in\mathbb R^m:\ (a_i-t,1,u_i)\in K_{\exp}\ \text{for every }i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m u_i\le1.\]
Substituting the appropriate affine arguments yields exponential-cone formulations of binary and multiclass logistic-loss epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log-sum-exp epigraph is represented exactly using one exponential-cone constraint per exponential term and a single sum constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed exponential-cone system is equivalent to \(t\ge\log(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{a_i})\).
review_flags: Exact exponential-cone representation requires a directly supporting conic-optimization source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed exponential-cone definition and the stated log-sum-exp epigraph equivalence are coherent, and representation is the correct content kind. The exact cone convention and equivalence require a directly supporting conic-optimization source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy-Conjugate Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational representation of log-sum-exp through negative entropy on the probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(a\in\mathbb R^m\) and the simplex \(\Delta_m=\{p\in\mathbb R_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\}\),
\[\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{a_i}\right)=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m p_i a_i-\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\log p_i\right\},\]
where \(0\log0=0\). The maximizer is \(p_i=e^{a_i}/\sum_j e^{a_j}\). Consequently, logistic losses admit saddle or dual formulations by replacing each log-sum-exp term with this entropy variational form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-sum-exp is the convex conjugate of negative entropy restricted to the probability simplex, with softmax as its maximizing distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log(\sum_i e^{a_i})=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\{p^\top a-\sum_i p_i\log p_i\}\), attained by the softmax vector.
review_flags: The supplied conjugate-functions locator is too broad to certify this entropy identity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entropy variational identity and softmax maximizer are mathematically correct, and duality fits the terminal container. The local inventory's broad conjugate-functions entry is not cited by the record and does not specifically locate this identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Standard Binary Hinge Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-margin convex surrogate for binary classification with signed labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a binary label \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) and score \(f\in\mathbb R\), the standard binary hinge loss is
\[\ell_{\mathrm{hinge}}(y,f)=\max\{0,1-yf\}=(1-yf)_+.\]
It vanishes when the signed margin \(yf\) is at least one and otherwise decreases linearly with that margin. For fixed \(y\), it is a finite convex piecewise-affine function of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hinge loss is zero at signed margins of at least one and otherwise equals the unit-margin shortfall.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{hinge}}(y,f)=\max\{0,1-yf\}\) is convex and piecewise affine in \(f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Weighted Hinge Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary hinge loss with positive class-dependent misclassification costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\), let \(t\in\mathbb R\) be a score, and choose costs \(c_{-1},c_{+1}>0\). The cost-weighted hinge loss is \[\ell_c(y,t)=c_y\max\{0,1-yt\}.\] For fixed \(y\), the map \(t\mapsto\ell_c(y,t)\) is nonnegative, convex, and piecewise affine. It vanishes when \(yt\ge 1\), and a margin violation of size \(1-yt>0\) incurs that violation multiplied by the cost assigned to the observed class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary binary hinge loss is multiplied by a positive cost associated with the observed class, allowing asymmetric penalties while preserving convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_c(y,t)=c_y(1-yt)_+\) is convex in \(t\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic positive-part variant of binary hinge loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary label \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) and score \(t\in\mathbb R\), define the margin \(m=yt\). The squared hinge loss is \[\ell_{\mathrm{sq}}(y,t)=\bigl(\max\{0,1-m\}\bigr)^2.\] Equivalently, it equals \((1-m)^2\) when \(m<1\) and \(0\) when \(m\ge 1\). As a function of \(t\) for fixed \(y\), it is nonnegative, convex, continuously differentiable, and has derivative \(-2y(1-yt)\) on \(yt<1\) and \(0\) on \(yt\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared hinge loss squares the positive margin shortfall. It is nonnegative, convex, and continuously differentiable in the score.

Smoothed Hinge Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Huberized hinge family with smoothing width \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For margin \(m=yt\) and smoothing width \(\delta>0\), the Huberized hinge loss is \[h_\delta(m)=\begin{cases}0,&m\ge1,\\(1-m)^2/(2\delta),&1-\delta<m<1,\\1-m-\delta/2,&m\le1-\delta.\end{cases}\] The associated binary loss is \(\ell_\delta(y,t)=h_\delta(yt)\). The pieces agree in value and first derivative at both breakpoints, so \(h_\delta\) is convex and continuously differentiable. Its derivative is globally \(1/\delta\)-Lipschitz, and \(h_\delta(m)\) differs from the ordinary hinge \((1-m)_+\) by at most \(\delta/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Huberization replaces the hinge kink by a quadratic transition of width delta, producing a convex differentiable loss uniformly close to the original hinge.

knowledge_statements.title: Modified Huber Classification Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary modified-Huber surrogate in its standard margin normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary label \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\), score \(t\in\mathbb R\), and margin \(m=yt\), the modified Huber classification loss is \[\ell_{\mathrm{MH}}(y,t)=\begin{cases}0,&m\ge1,\\(1-m)^2,&-1\le m<1,\\-4m,&m<-1.\end{cases}\] The formulas match in value and derivative at \(m=-1\) and \(m=1\). knowledge_statements.title: Joint Multiclass Hinge Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crammer–Singer joint hinge using the largest competing-class violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\ge2\), let the true class be \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), and let \(s\in\mathbb R^K\) be the score vector. The unit-margin joint multiclass hinge loss is \[\ell_{\mathrm{joint}}(y,s)=\max\!\left\{0,\max_{j\ne y}\bigl(1+s_j-s_y\bigr)\right\}.\] It is the maximum of finitely many affine functions of \(s\), hence is convex and polyhedral. It vanishes exactly when \(s_y\ge s_j+1\) for every competing class \(j\ne y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The joint multiclass hinge penalizes only the largest positive unit-margin violation among all classes competing with the true class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{joint}}(y,s)\) is convex and vanishes exactly under all unit-margin inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Multiclass Hinge Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sum of true-versus-competing-class hinge penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\ge2\), \(y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), and \(s\in\mathbb R^K\). A unit-margin pairwise multiclass hinge loss is \[\ell_{\mathrm{pair}}(y,s)=\sum_{j\ne y}\max\{0,1+s_j-s_y\}.\] Each summand compares the true class with one competitor. Therefore the loss is convex and polyhedral in \(s\), and it vanishes exactly when \(s_y\ge s_j+1\) for all \(j\ne y\). Division by \(K-1\) gives the commonly used averaged normalization without changing its minimizers under fixed \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise multiclass hinge loss sums the positive unit-margin violations between the true class and each competing class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{pair}}(y,s)\) is convex, polyhedral, and zero precisely when all pairwise unit margins hold.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss-augmented margin-rescaling hinge for finite structured output spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be an input set, let \(x\in\mathcal X\), let \(\mathcal Y\) be a finite output set, let \(y\in\mathcal Y\) be observed, and let \(w\in\mathbb R^p\). Suppose \(F(x,y';w)\) is affine in \(w\) for every \(y'\in\mathcal Y\), and let \(\Delta(y,y')\ge0\) for every \(y'\in\mathcal Y\), with \(\Delta(y,y)=0\). The margin-rescaling structured hinge loss is \[\ell_{\mathrm{str}}(w;x,y)=\max_{y'\in\mathcal Y}\left\{\Delta(y,y')+F(x,y';w)-F(x,y;w)\right\}.\] It is convex and polyhedral in \(w\). It vanishes exactly when \(F(x,y;w)-F(x,y';w)\ge\Delta(y,y')\) for every \(y'\in\mathcal Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The margin-rescaling structured hinge takes the largest task-loss-augmented score advantage of any candidate output over the observed output. For a finite output space and scores affine in the parameter vector, it is convex and polyhedral in that vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard-margin formulation and its geometric maximum-margin interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge1\), and let \((x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb R^d\times\{-1,+1\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Suppose there exist \(w\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\) such that \(y_i(\langle w,x_i\rangle+b)>0\) for every \(i\). Rescaling a strict separator permits the functional-margin constraints \(y_i(\langle w,x_i\rangle+b)\ge1\). The hard-margin problem \[\min_{w\in\mathbb R^d,\,b\in\mathbb R}\ \frac12\lVert w\rVert_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(\langle w,x_i\rangle+b)\ge1\quad\text{for }i=1,\ldots,n\] maximizes the sample geometric margin \(\min_{1\le i\le n}y_i(\langle w,x_i\rangle+b)/\lVert w\rVert_2\) among separating affine classifiers.

knowledge_statements.title: Margin-Maximum Route
Slack-Epigraph Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph reformulation of regularized empirical binary hinge minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \((x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb R^d\times\{-1,+1\}\) and \(\lambda>0\), the unconstrained hinge problem \[\min_{w,b}\ \frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert w\rVert_2^2+\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\max\{0,1-y_i(\langle w,x_i\rangle+b)\}\] has the equivalent epigraph form \[\min_{w,b,\xi}\ \frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert w\rVert_2^2+\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad \xi_i\ge0,\quad \xi_i\ge1-y_i(\langle w,x_i\rangle+b).\] At every optimum, each \(\xi_i\) equals the corresponding hinge loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introducing one nonnegative slack per example converts regularized hinge minimization into an equivalent convex quadratic program with linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unconstrained and slack-epigraph programs have equal optimal values and corresponding optimal \((w,b)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Conjugate Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel support representation of the scalar hinge function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h(z)=\max\{0,1-z\}\) for \(z\in\mathbb R\). Its Fenchel conjugate is \[h^*(u)=\begin{cases}u,&-1\le u\le0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\] Hence Fenchel biconjugacy gives the polyhedral representation \[h(z)=\sup_{u\in[-1,0]}\{uz-u\}=\sup_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\alpha(1-z).\] The supremum is attained at \(\alpha=1\) when \(z<1\), at \(\alpha=0\) when \(z>1\), and by every \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) when \(z=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hinge is the support maximum of affine functions indexed by the unit interval; its conjugate is affine on a compact interval and infinite elsewhere.

notation.meaning: zero on the interval and positive infinity outside it

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Exponential Margin Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical exponential surrogate for binary signed margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary label \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) and score \(t\in\mathbb R\), define the signed margin \(m=yt\). The binary exponential margin loss is \[\ell_{\exp}(y,t)=\exp(-yt)=\exp(-m).\] For fixed \(y\), it is strictly positive, strictly convex, and infinitely differentiable in \(t\), with derivative \(-y\exp(-yt)\) and second derivative \(\exp(-yt)>0\). It decreases to zero as the positive margin tends to infinity and grows exponentially as the margin tends to negative infinity.

children.top_down_role: Cross-family modeling choices that modify how per-observation losses are combined without introducing regularizers or optimization algorithms.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\ge 1\) observations with prediction variables \(z_i\in\mathcal Z_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Loss Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats coupling as failure of additive coordinate decomposition on the stated product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Z=\mathcal Z_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal Z_d\). A loss \(L:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) has coupled aggregation across coordinates if there do not exist a constant \(c\in\mathbb R\) and functions \(\phi_j:\mathcal Z_j\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \[L(z_1,\ldots,z_d)=c+\sum_{j=1}^d\phi_j(z_j)\] throughout \(\mathcal Z\). For a twice continuously differentiable finite loss on an open connected product domain, any nonzero mixed partial \(\frac{\partial^2L}{\partial z_j\partial z_k}\) with \(j\ne k\) certifies such coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled aggregation means the loss cannot be written as a constant plus independent coordinate losses; a nonzero mixed second derivative certifies coupling for smooth losses.
assumptions_latex: The decision is \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\) in the product domain \(\mathcal Z=\mathcal Z_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal Z_d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The loss is coupled when no additive representation \(L(z)=c+\sum_{j=1}^d\phi_j(z_j)\) exists on its domain.

children.title: Structured-Output Aggregation

assumptions_latex: The structured label space \(\mathcal Y\) is finite.
A model assigns scores \(s_y\in\mathbb R\) to all \(y\in\mathcal Y\).
The task cost satisfies \(\Delta:\mathcal Y\times\mathcal Y\to[0,+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A canonical structured aggregate is \(L(s,y)=\max_{y'\in\mathcal Y}\{\Delta(y,y')+s_{y'}-s_y\}\), which jointly compares the observed structure with all alternatives.

As a pointwise maximum of affine functions of \(s\), \(L_{\mathrm{str}}(\cdot,y)\) is convex; it is generally coordinate-coupled.

children.title: Structure-Induced Coupling

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Induced Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a finite factor representation to distinguish local structural interactions from full coordinate separability while allowing cancellation among overlapping factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=(z_v)_{v\in V}\) and let \(F\) be a family of factors \(\alpha\subseteq V\). A structure-induced loss may have the factor representation \[L(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in F}\psi_\alpha(z_\alpha),\] where \(z_\alpha=(z_v)_{v\in\alpha}\). If every factor is a singleton, then \(L\) is coordinate-separable. More generally, the structure induces coupling precisely when the total aggregate \(L\) cannot be expressed as a constant plus a sum of one-coordinate functions. A nonseparable factor involving at least two coordinates establishes such coupling only when its interaction is not canceled by the remaining factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor representation can induce coordinate coupling through multi-coordinate interactions, but coupling is a property of the total loss because interactions from overlapping factors can cancel.
assumptions_latex: The prediction has components indexed by a finite set \(V\).
A structure is represented by a finite family of factors \(F\subseteq 2^V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The factorized aggregate \(L(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in F}\psi_\alpha(z_\alpha)\) is structure-induced coupled exactly when the total aggregate has no additive one-coordinate decomposition; an uncanceled nonseparable multi-coordinate factor is sufficient.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: factor representations describe interactions induced by structured dependencies, subject to possible cancellation across factors

knowledge_statements.title: Observation-Weighted Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weights observations, not classes; a zero-weighted loss term is defined to be identically zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given losses \(\ell_i:\mathcal Z_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and fixed weights \(w_i\ge 0\), define \(w_i\ell_i\equiv 0\) when \(w_i=0\). The observation-weighted aggregate is \[L_w(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\ell_i(z_i).\] When \(W=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i>0\), the normalized convention is \(W^{-1}L_w\). If every \(\ell_i\) is convex, then both aggregates are convex. Multiplying all weights by the same positive constant changes only the global scale of the unnormalized objective, whereas changing their relative values changes the observations' relative influence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Observation-weighted loss multiplies each sample loss by a fixed nonnegative weight, with a zero-weighted term defined to vanish; normalization by total weight changes scale but not relative influence.
assumptions_latex: Weights satisfy \(w_i\ge 0\) and are fixed independently of the optimization variables.
For \(w_i=0\), the weighted term \(w_i\ell_i\) is defined to be identically zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observation-weighted aggregate is \(L_w=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\ell_i\), or its weight-normalized version when \(\sum_iw_i>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_K)\) with \(a_k\ge 0\). If \(\ell(\cdot,y)\) is convex for every \(y\), then \(\ell_a(\cdot,y)\) and \(L_a\) are convex.

children.title: Singular-Covariance Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural limitations of covariance-based normalization under degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Covariance Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the rank-deficient boundary of exact full-dimensional covariance whitening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\) be a centered random vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with covariance \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}_+^d\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)<d\). No matrix \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) can satisfy \(W\Sigma W^{\mathsf T}=I_d\), because \(\operatorname{rank}(W\Sigma W^{\mathsf T})\leq\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)<d\). Pseudoinverse normalization gives \(\Sigma^{\dagger/2}\Sigma\Sigma^{\dagger/2}=P_{\operatorname{range}(\Sigma)}\), so \(\operatorname{Cov}(\Sigma^{\dagger/2}r)=P_{\operatorname{range}(\Sigma)}\). The associated seminorm \(r^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^\dagger r\) ignores components in \(\ker(\Sigma)\). Replacing \(\Sigma\) by \(\Sigma+\lambda I_d\), where \(\lambda>0\), restores invertibility but changes the normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular covariance cannot be whitened to the full identity. Pseudoinverse normalization produces identity covariance only on the covariance range and ignores null-space components.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is a random vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[r]=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Cov}(\Sigma^{\dagger/2}r)=P_{\operatorname{range}(\Sigma)}\neq I_d,\] and no \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) satisfies \(W\Sigma W^{\mathsf T}=I_d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Margin-Scale Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines positive scalar normalization for binary signed margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(y_i\in\{-1,1\}\), and \(f_i\in\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Margin-scale normalization replaces the signed margin \(y_i f_i\) by \(m_i=y_i f_i/s\), where \(s>0\). For a convex function \(\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), the normalized empirical loss is \(L_s(f)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(y_i f_i/s)\), where \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For fixed \(s\), \(L_s\) is convex in \(f\). Changing \(s\) changes the effective transition width and is not generally equivalent to multiplying the objective by a constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide each binary signed margin by a positive scale before applying a convex margin loss. For a fixed scale the empirical loss remains convex, while the scale controls its transition width.

knowledge_statements.title: Response-Outlier Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Response-direction robustness boundary of unbounded squared loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a probability distribution on \(\mathbb{R}\) with finite mean \(T(F)=\int y\,dF(y)\). For squared loss \(\ell(y,a)=(y-a)^2\), the derivative \(\partial_a\ell(y,a)=2(a-y)\) is unbounded in \(y\). Given \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\) and \(z\in\mathbb{R}\), define \(F_{\varepsilon,z}=(1-\varepsilon)F+\varepsilon\delta_z\). Its mean target is \(T(F_{\varepsilon,z})=(1-\varepsilon)T(F)+\varepsilon z\), so \(|T(F_{\varepsilon,z})|\) is unbounded as \(|z|\to\infty\). Squared-loss mean fitting therefore has unbounded response-outlier sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For squared-loss mean fitting, an arbitrarily extreme contaminated response causes an arbitrarily large score and can move the population target without bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a probability distribution on \(\mathbb{R}\) with finite mean \(T(F)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), both \(2|a-z|\) and \(\left|T(F_{\varepsilon,z})\right|\) can be made arbitrarily large by increasing \(|z|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Leverage Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Design-direction robustness boundary for unbounded covariates in linear squared-loss fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\beta,x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), let \(\ell_\beta(x,y)=(y-x^{\mathsf T}\beta)^2\). Its per-observation gradient is \(\nabla_\beta\ell_\beta(x,y)=2x(x^{\mathsf T}\beta-y)\). This gradient is not uniformly bounded over \((x,y)\). In particular, for any fixed nonzero residual \(c\), choosing a sequence \(x_k\) with \(\|x_k\|_2\to\infty\) and \(y_k=x_k^{\mathsf T}\beta-c\) gives \(\|\nabla_\beta\ell_\beta(x_k,y_k)\|_2=2|c|\|x_k\|_2\to\infty\). Thus an extreme design point can exert arbitrarily large first-order influence through the multiplicative covariate factor.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness–Efficiency Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian location efficiency versus bounded-influence robustness for regular location M-estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_i=\theta+\sigma Z_i\), where \(Z_i\) are independent standard normal variables, and let \(\widehat\theta_n\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^n\psi((X_i-\widehat\theta_n)/\sigma)=0\). Under regularity conditions ensuring asymptotic normality and Gaussian integration by parts, the asymptotic variance factor relative to the Gaussian location bound is \[V(\psi)=\frac{\mathbb E[\psi(Z)^2]}{(\mathbb E[\psi'(Z)])^2}\ge 1.\] Equality holds only if \(\psi(Z)=cZ\) almost surely for some nonzero constant \(c\). Consequently, a bounded score with nonzero \(\mathbb E[\psi'(Z)]\) has \(V(\psi)>1\) and therefore cannot attain full Gaussian efficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded score limits gross-error influence but has strictly larger asymptotic variance than the Gaussian-efficient linear score.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[\psi(Z)^2]<\infty\), with regularity sufficient for Gaussian integration by parts and M-estimator asymptotics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(\psi)\ge 1\), and bounded \(\psi\) implies \(V(\psi)>1\).

notation.meaning: asymptotic variance factor relative to the Gaussian location bound

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Least Squares
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional unregularized linear least squares with a rank-deficient design matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), every minimizer of \(x\mapsto \tfrac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2\) satisfies the normal equations \(A^{\mathsf T}Ax=A^{\mathsf T}b\), and the complete minimizer set is \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^p}\frac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2=A^\dagger b+\ker A=\{A^\dagger b+(I-A^\dagger A)z:z\in\mathbb R^p\}.\] Thus the fitted vector is uniquely \(AA^\dagger b\), while the coefficient vector is nonunique exactly when \(\ker A\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank deficiency leaves the fitted response unique but makes every null-space displacement of the pseudoinverse solution another least-squares minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}\tfrac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2=A^\dagger b+\ker A\), with uniqueness iff \(\ker A=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Median Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimizer set of the finite-sample absolute-deviation location loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(n)}\) be the ordered observations. The minimizers of the absolute-deviation objective are \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{m\in\mathbb R}\sum_{i=1}^n|y_i-m|=\begin{cases}\{y_{((n+1)/2)}\},&n\text{ odd},\\[y_{(n/2)},y_{(n/2+1)}],&n\text{ even}.\end{cases}\] Consequently, the sample median is nonunique precisely when \(n\) is even and \(y_{(n/2)}<y_{(n/2+1)}\); then every point between the two central order statistics has the same minimum loss.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The median minimizer set is non-singleton iff \(n\) is even and \(y_{(n/2)}<y_{(n/2+1)}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Quantile Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population quantiles as minimizers of expected pinball loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\tau\in(0,1)\), let \(Y\) be integrable with distribution function \(F\), and define \(\rho_\tau(u)=u(\tau-\mathbf 1_{\{u<0\}})\). Then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E\rho_\tau(Y-q)=\{q\in\mathbb R:F(q-)\le\tau\le F(q)\}.\] This set is a closed interval, possibly a singleton. The population \(\tau\)-quantile is nonunique exactly when two distinct real numbers satisfy these inequalities, in which case the entire interval between them minimizes the expected pinball loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected pinball loss is minimized by every point whose left and right distribution probabilities bracket the target quantile level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{q}\mathbb E\rho_\tau(Y-q)=\{q:F(q-)\le\tau\le F(q)\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Mass Tie Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional condition producing an interval of population quantiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\tau\in(0,1)\), an interval of tied \(\tau\)-quantiles occurs exactly when there exist \(a<b\) such that \[\mathbb P(Y\le a)=\tau=\mathbb P(Y<b).\] Equivalently, the distribution assigns no probability to \((a,b)\) and its cumulative probability throughout that gap equals \(\tau\). Under this condition every \(q\in[a,b]\) satisfies \(F(q-)\le\tau\le F(q)\) and minimizes expected pinball loss. Conversely, any two distinct population \(\tau\)-quantiles yield such a probability-free interval between suitable endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quantile ties arise when the cumulative probability equals the target level across a nonempty gap containing no probability mass.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a real-valued random variable and \(\tau\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nondegenerate quantile interval exists iff \(\mathbb P(Y\le a)=\mathbb P(Y<b)=\tau\) for some \(a<b\).

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Logistic Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous formulation; an intercept may be included as a coordinate of each design vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \((x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb R^p\times\{-1,1\}\), complete logistic separation holds when there exists a direction \(d\in\mathbb R^p\) such that \[y_i x_i^{\mathsf T}d>0\qquad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,n.\] Equivalently, the two labeled classes lie strictly on opposite sides of the hyperplane determined by \(d\), using an augmented coordinate when an intercept is fitted. Along \(\beta_t=td\), every signed margin tends to positive infinity and every term of the unregularized logistic loss tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete separation means one coefficient direction gives every observation a strictly positive signed margin, allowing logistic loss to approach zero at diverging coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete separation is the existence of \(d\) satisfying \(y_i x_i^{\mathsf T}d>0\) for all \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Complete Logistic Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary logistic separation allowing observations on the separating hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \((x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb R^p\times\{-1,1\}\), quasi-complete separation holds when there exists a nonzero direction \(d\) satisfying \[y_i x_i^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\quad\text{for all }i,\qquad y_jx_j^{\mathsf T}d>0\quad\text{for at least one }j,\] but no direction has strictly positive signed margin for every observation. Thus some observations remain on the separating hyperplane while none crosses to the wrong side. The final exclusion distinguishes quasi-complete from complete separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-complete separation has a direction with no negative signed margins and at least one positive margin, but no direction makes all margins positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quasi-complete separation is weak separation with at least one strict margin, excluding complete separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Optimizer Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment of unregularized empirical logistic loss along a separating recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1+\exp(-y_i x_i^{\mathsf T}\beta))\). If a nonzero \(d\) satisfies \(y_i x_i^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) for every \(i\) and the inequality is strict for at least one observation, then for every finite \(\beta\), \(L(\beta+td)\) decreases strictly as \(t\to\infty\) and converges to a finite limit. Therefore no finite \(\beta\) attains the infimum. Under complete separation that infimum is \(0\); under quasi-complete separation, zero-margin observations may leave a positive limiting loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separating recession direction strictly lowers logistic loss indefinitely, so the infimum is approached only by coefficients diverging to infinity.
assumptions_latex: The logistic objective is unregularized and finite-dimensional.
There exists \(d\ne0\) with all signed directional margins nonnegative and at least one positive.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Margin Minimizer Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimizer geometry for a nonnegative margin loss with a zero-valued flat tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\) be convex and satisfy \(\phi(u)=0\) exactly when \(u\ge\gamma\). For labeled data \((x_i,y_i)\), define \(R(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(y_i x_i^{\mathsf T}\beta)\). If the margin-feasible polyhedron \(C=\{\beta:y_i x_i^{\mathsf T}\beta\ge\gamma\text{ for all }i\}\) is nonempty, then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb R^p}R(\beta)=C,\qquad \min R=0.\] Hence lack of strict convexity on the attained margin range produces a generally nonunique, possibly unbounded, minimizer set.
