knowledge_statements.title: Classification-Calibration Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary classification calibration for nonnegative convex margin losses differentiable at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in\{-1,1\}\), let \(\eta=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid X=x)\), and use the surrogate loss \(\ell(y,f)=\phi(yf)\), where \(\phi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\) is convex and differentiable at \(0\). Define the conditional surrogate risk by \(C_\eta(f)=\eta\phi(f)+(1-\eta)\phi(-f)\). This convex margin loss is classification-calibrated for the zero-one Bayes decision if and only if \[\phi'(0)<0.\] Under this condition, whenever \(\eta\ne\tfrac12\), every conditional-risk minimizer has the sign of \(2\eta-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative convex margin loss differentiable at zero, a negative derivative at zero exactly characterizes calibration to the Bayes binary classifier.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\) is convex and differentiable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classification calibration holds if and only if \(\phi'(0)<0\).

notation.meaning: conditional surrogate risk at class probability eta

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Estimation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hinge loss illustrates that classification calibration does not imply probability identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For hinge loss \(\phi(u)=(1-u)_+\), the binary conditional risk at class probability \(\eta\) is \[C_\eta(f)=\eta(1-f)_+ +(1-\eta)(1+f)_+.\] Its minimizer set is \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{f\in\mathbb R}C_\eta(f)=\begin{cases}\{1\},&\eta>\tfrac12,\\[-1,1],&\eta=\tfrac12,\\\{-1\},&\eta<\tfrac12.\end{cases}\] Thus hinge-risk minimization identifies the Bayes class sign away from \(\eta=\tfrac12\), but its optimal score contains no information about the magnitude of \(\eta\). Classification calibration alone therefore does not ensure calibrated probability estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hinge loss recovers which class is more probable but maps every probability on the same side of one-half to the same optimal score.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hinge loss is classification-calibrated but does not identify \(\eta\) from its conditional-risk minimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Threshold Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary probability thresholding under unequal false-positive and false-negative costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\eta(x)=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid X=x)\), with false-positive cost \(c_{\mathrm{FP}}>0\) and false-negative cost \(c_{\mathrm{FN}}>0\). Define \[t^*=\frac{c_{\mathrm{FP}}}{c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}}}.\] Conditional risk is minimized by predicting class \(1\) when \(\eta(x)>t^*\), by predicting class \(0\) when \(\eta(x)<t^*\), and by either prediction when \(\eta(x)=t^*\). Thus the default threshold \(1/2\) need not implement the cost-sensitive Bayes rule when the costs are unequal. Wherever the default and Bayes decisions disagree, the conditional excess cost is \((c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}})|\eta(x)-t^*|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal error costs shift the Bayes probability threshold away from one-half; either decision is optimal exactly at the shifted threshold, and using one-half incurs excess cost where the decisions differ.
assumptions_latex: The prediction rule minimizes conditional expected misclassification cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cost-sensitive Bayes threshold is \(t^*=c_{\mathrm{FP}}/(c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}})\), with both decisions optimal when \(\eta(x)=t^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Label-Noise Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary margin losses under independent symmetric label noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y\in\{-1,1\}\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\ell(Y,f(X))=\phi(Yf(X))\). Suppose \(\widetilde Y=-Y\) with probability \(\rho\in[0,1/2)\), independently of \((X,Y)\). Then
\[
R_\rho(f)=(1-\rho)\mathbb E[\phi(Yf(X))]+\rho\mathbb E[\phi(-Yf(X))].
\]
If \(\eta(x)=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid X=x)\), then \(\widetilde\eta(x)=\rho+(1-2\rho)\eta(x)\), so the Bayes classification sign is preserved. A general surrogate-risk minimizer need not be preserved; invariance follows, for example, when \(\phi(t)+\phi(-t)\) is constant because then \(R_\rho(f)=(1-2\rho)R_0(f)+\rho C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric label noise preserves the Bayes sign but can change a surrogate-risk minimizer unless the loss has a suitable symmetry, such as a constant sum at opposite margins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde\eta-1/2=(1-2\rho)(\eta-1/2)\), while surrogate minimizer invariance requires additional loss structure.

notation.meaning: Population surrogate risk under noise level rho.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral conditioning of full-column-rank linear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L(x)=\tfrac12\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2\) with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the gradient and Hessian are
\[
\nabla L(x)=A^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b),\qquad \nabla^2L(x)=A^{\mathsf T}A.
\]
If \(A\) has full column rank, then \(L\) is \(\sigma_{\min}(A)^2\)-strongly convex and has \(\sigma_{\max}(A)^2\)-Lipschitz gradient. Its spectral condition number is \(\kappa_2(A^{\mathsf T}A)=\kappa_2(A)^2\). Thus forming normal equations squares the conditioning; if \(A\) is rank deficient, the Hessian is singular and this condition number is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The least-squares Hessian is the normal matrix. Its condition number is the square of that of the design matrix, and rank deficiency makes it singular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(\nabla^2L)=\kappa_2(A)^2\) when \(A\) has full column rank.

children.title: Kink-Point Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Evaluation behavior at nondifferentiable points of convex losses.

knowledge_statements.title: Kink-Point Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact evaluation and active-piece identification for convex piecewise-smooth losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\ell(z)=\max_{1\leq j\leq r}\ell_j(z)\), where every \(\ell_j:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable. At any evaluation point \(z\), compute
\[
\ell(z)=\max_j\ell_j(z),\qquad I(z)=\{j:\ell_j(z)=\ell(z)\}.
\]
The point is a kink whenever the active gradients are not all equal. Its complete first-order evaluation is
\[
\partial\ell(z)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla\ell_j(z):j\in I(z)\}.
\]
Consequently, evaluating only one active branch gives the correct value but may discard valid directional information at a tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a maximum-of-pieces kink, evaluate all tied active pieces. The value is their common maximum, and the subdifferential is the convex hull of their gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_j\) is convex and differentiable for every \(j\).
The maximum contains finitely many pieces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\ell(z)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla\ell_j(z):j\in I(z)\}\).

notation.meaning: Indices of pieces attaining the maximum at the evaluation point.

children.title: Tied-Score Handling
children.top_down_role: Numerical interpretation of equal residuals, margins, or class scores.

knowledge_statements.title: Tied-Score Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit randomized convention for binary decisions at a score threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s:X\to\mathbb R\) be a binary score with threshold \(\tau\), and fix \(q\in[0,1]\). Define the threshold decision by
\[
\mathbb P(h_{\tau,q}(x)=1)=
\begin{cases}
1,&s(x)>\tau,\\
q,&s(x)=\tau,\\
0,&s(x)<\tau.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(q=1\), \(q=0\), and \(q=1/2\) encode positive, negative, and uniform-random tie breaking. If \(\eta(x)=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid X=x)\), the conditional zero-one risk at a tied score is \(q(1-\eta(x))+(1-q)\eta(x)\). Reporting \(q\) makes the classifier and its risk well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold classifier must specify what happens at equality. A parameter q records positive, negative, or randomized tie breaking and determines the tie-point classification risk.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in[0,1]\) is fixed independently of the unknown label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(s(x)=\tau\), the conditional error is \(q(1-\eta(x))+(1-q)\eta(x)\).

notation.meaning: Probability of predicting the positive class at a tie.

children.title: Subgradient Ambiguity at Kinks
children.top_down_role: Local ambiguity in valid slope selections at nonsmooth loss points.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Ambiguity at Kinks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of valid first-order directions at a convex kink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). At a kink, \(\partial f(x)\) may contain multiple vectors. Every \(g\in\partial f(x)\) satisfies
\[
f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\text{for all }y\in\mathbb R^d,
\]
but distinct choices can produce distinct subgradient steps \(x^+=x-\alpha g\). The choice is therefore algorithmic data, not a uniquely determined derivative. Optimality is unambiguous: \(x\) minimizes \(f\) globally if and only if \(0\in\partial f(x)\), regardless of which nonzero subgradient an implementation returns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a convex kink, several subgradients may be valid and yield different updates. The invariant optimality test is membership of zero in the entire subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname*{argmin} f\) if and only if \(0\in\partial f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Stable Logistic-Loss Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overflow-resistant scalar evaluation of binary logistic loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a binary margin \(m=ys\), the logistic loss admits the exact representation
\[
\ell(m)=\log(1+e^{-m})=\max\{0,-m\}+\log\!\left(1+e^{-|m|}\right).
\]
The right-hand expression evaluates the exponential only at the nonpositive argument \(-|m|\), preventing overflow when \(m\) is a large negative number. In floating-point arithmetic it should be implemented as \(\max\{0,-m\}+\operatorname{log1p}(\exp(-|m|))\). Its derivative may be evaluated stably as \(-1/(1+e^m)\) for \(m\leq0\) and \(-e^{-m}/(1+e^{-m})\) for \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rewrite logistic loss using the absolute margin and log1p so exponentiation uses a nonpositive argument. A sign-split derivative similarly avoids overflow.
assumptions_latex: Floating-point functions \(\operatorname{log1p}\) and \(\exp\) follow their usual stable implementations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log(1+e^{-m})=\max\{0,-m\}+\operatorname{log1p}(e^{-|m|})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Loss-Magnitude Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of positive loss rescaling on minimizers, gradients, and regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R(f)=\mathbb E[\ell(Y,f(X))]\), and replace \(\ell\) by \(\widetilde\ell=a\ell\) for \(a>0\). Then \(\widetilde R=aR\), so
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{f\in\mathcal F}\widetilde R(f)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{f\in\mathcal F}R(f).
\]
Whenever the relevant derivatives exist, gradients and Hessians are multiplied by \(a\); for convex nonsmooth losses, \(\partial\widetilde R(f)=a\partial R(f)\). With a regularizer \(\Omega\), minimizing \(aR(f)+\lambda\Omega(f)\) is equivalent to minimizing \(R(f)+(\lambda/a)\Omega(f)\). Hence loss scaling preserves an unregularized optimizer but changes effective step sizes, tolerances, and regularization unless those quantities are rescaled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scaling leaves unregularized minimizers unchanged but scales first- and second-order information. With regularization, it changes the effective regularization coefficient unless lambda is adjusted.
assumptions_latex: The displayed expectations are finite on \(\mathcal F\).
\(\Omega\) is fixed under the loss rescaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}aR=\operatorname*{argmin}R\), while \(aR+\lambda\Omega\) has effective coefficient \(\lambda/a\).

children.title: Unit Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between response units, residual units, and reported loss values.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensional compatibility of additive objective terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an objective
\[
J(\theta)=\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k L_k(\theta)+\lambda\Omega(\theta).
\]
It is unit-consistent precisely when every additive term has the same physical dimension: for some objective unit \(U_J\),
\[
[\alpha_k][L_k]=U_J\quad(1\leq k\leq K),\qquad [\lambda][\Omega]=U_J.
\]
For a residual measured in unit \(U\), absolute loss has unit \(U\), whereas squared loss has unit \(U^2\); their coefficients must therefore carry different reciprocal units if the terms are combined. Adding quantities with unequal dimensions makes the numerical tradeoff depend on the arbitrary measurement unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All terms added in an objective must have the same physical dimension. Absolute and squared residual losses have different units and therefore require differently dimensioned weights.
assumptions_latex: Each modeled quantity is assigned a physical dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unit consistency holds exactly when \([\alpha_k][L_k]=[\lambda][\Omega]=U_J\) for every \(k\).

notation.meaning: Common physical dimension of the objective terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Family Scale Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence of intrinsic numerical comparability between differently normalized loss families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_i(f)=\mathbb E[\ell_i(Y,f(X))]\) for two loss families. Each replacement \(\ell_i\mapsto a_i\ell_i+b_i\), with \(a_i>0\) and constant \(b_i\), preserves the minimizers of \(R_i\) considered separately. However, it changes the weighted joint criterion
\[
J(f)=w_1R_1(f)+w_2R_2(f)
\]
unless the weights are transformed as \(w_i\mapsto w_i/a_i\); additive constants affect reported levels but not minimizers. Therefore raw magnitudes from different loss families have no intrinsic common scale. Their comparison requires an explicit normalization, reference distribution, or decision-relevant calibration fixed before optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate loss families may be rescaled without changing their own minimizers, so their raw values are not inherently comparable. Weighted combinations require explicit normalization or compensating weights.
assumptions_latex: All risks are finite on the compared class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-family weighted tradeoffs are invariant only when loss rescaling is accompanied by \(w_i\mapsto w_i/a_i\).
